column1: 1:1|The oracle that Habakkuk the prophet saw.|Retains the vision verb and prophetic oracle label.

1:2|How long, LORD, must I cry for help
while you do not listen?
I cry out to you, “Violence!”
but you do not save.|Makes the complaint audible without resolving its accusation against divine inaction.

1:3|Why do you make me see wrongdoing
and look on at misery?
Destruction and violence confront me;
strife breaks out and conflict rises.|Preserves the change from the prophet seeing to God looking and the escalating conflict.

1:4|So instruction is paralyzed,
and justice never prevails.
The wicked surround the righteous;
that is why justice comes out twisted.|Connects the repeated consequence while retaining instruction and distorted justice.

1:5|“Look among the nations! Look closely!
Be utterly astonished!
For a work is being done in your days
that you would not believe if told.|Keeps the plural summons and the work’s initially unexpressed agent.

1:6|I am raising up the Chaldeans,
that bitter, headlong nation,
who march across the breadth of the earth
to seize homes that are not theirs.|Retains Chaldeans and the concrete seizure of others’ homes.
1:7|They are frightening and fearsome;\ntheir justice and authority come from themselves.|Keeps the accusation of self-authorized rule without supplying modern political labels.

1:8|Their horses are faster than leopards,
fiercer than wolves at dusk.
Their horsemen spread out;
their horsemen come from far away,
flying like an eagle rushing to feed.|Retains both horsemen clauses and the predator images.
1:9|They all come for violence,\ntheir faces pressing eastward.\nThey gather captives like sand.|Follows the difficult eastward wording provisionally and preserves the innumerable captives image.

1:10|They mock kings
and laugh at rulers.
They laugh at every fortress,
heap up earth, and capture it.|Preserves repeated laughter and the concrete siege-ramp action.
1:11|Then they sweep on like the wind and pass through—\nguilty people, whose strength is their god.”|Takes wind as comparison and keeps guilt attached to the invader’s self-deification.

1:12|Are you not from ancient times,
LORD my God, my Holy One?
We will not die.
LORD, you appointed them for judgment;
Rock, you established them for correction.|Keeps the pinned we-will-not-die reading and both divine titles.

1:13|Your eyes are too pure to look on evil;
you cannot gaze at misery.
Why, then, do you look on at traitors
and stay silent when the wicked swallow
those more righteous than themselves?|Preserves the deliberate tension between inability to look and looking on.
1:14|You make human beings like fish in the sea,\nlike crawling creatures with no ruler.|Retains God as grammatical agent and human vulnerability in the animal comparison.

1:15|The enemy hauls them all up with a hook,
drags them in his net,
gathers them in his dragnet.
That is why he rejoices and celebrates.|Identifies the continuing hostile singular figure for readers and retains all fishing implements.

1:16|That is why he sacrifices to his net
and burns incense to his dragnet:
through them his share is rich
and his food plentiful.|Connects idolatrous worship to material benefit without turning the metaphor into explanation.
1:17|Will he keep emptying his net, then,\nand killing nations without mercy?|Keeps the unresolved closing question and repeated predation.

2:1|I will stand at my watchpost
and take my place on the rampart.
I will watch to see what he says to me
and how I should answer about my complaint.|Retains first-person answer rather than changing it to God’s answer; notes the final clause’s difficulty.

2:2|The LORD answered me:
“Write the vision;
make it plain on tablets,
so the one who reads it can run.|Keeps the running reader image without choosing reading-on-the-run or messenger exclusively.

2:3|The vision is still for its appointed time.
It presses toward the end and will not lie.
If it delays, wait for it;
it will surely come. It will not be late.|Retains the deliberate delay/not-late tension and the certain coming.

2:4|Look at the swollen one—\nhis life within him is not upright.\nBut the righteous will live by their faithfulness.|Preserves the difficult swollen description and personal faithfulness, with faith’s range noted.

2:5|Wine, too, betrays.
The arrogant man will not stay at rest.
He opens his appetite as wide as Sheol;
like death, he is never satisfied.
He gathers all nations to himself
and collects all peoples.|Follows pinned wine rather than an emendation and retains Sheol and insatiable conquest.

2:6|Will not all of them take up a taunt against him,
a mocking riddle, and say:
‘Woe to the one who piles up what is not his—
how long?—
and loads himself with pledges!’|Keeps the embedded how-long cry and ambiguous debt/pledge image.
2:7|Will not your creditors suddenly rise?\nWill not those who make you tremble wake up?\nThen you will become their plunder.|Retains the reversal and notes the biting/creditor wordplay.

2:8|Because you plundered many nations,
all the peoples left will plunder you—
for human bloodshed and violence against the land,
the city, and all who live in it.|Maintains repeated plunder and the full refrain of harmed places and people.
2:9|Woe to the one who makes evil profit for his house,\nsetting his nest high\nto escape the reach of harm!|Keeps house/nest relation and the ironic attempt to secure safety through harm.
2:10|You have planned shame for your own house\nby cutting off many peoples;\nyou have sinned against your own life.|Retains the reflexive cost of the oppressor’s plan.
2:11|A stone will cry out from the wall,\nand a timber beam will answer it.|Preserves the building materials as speaking witnesses.
2:12|Woe to the one who builds a town with bloodshed\nand establishes a city through injustice!|Keeps both building clauses and distinct bloodshed/injustice terms.

2:13|Is this not from the LORD of Armies:\npeoples labor only to feed the fire,\nand nations exhaust themselves for nothing?|Makes the rhetorical question readable while retaining the destruction of labor’s results.
2:14|For the earth will be filled\nwith knowledge of the LORD’s glory,\nas waters cover the sea.|Retains the recognizable image and glory rather than forcing novelty.

2:15|Woe to the one who makes his neighbor drink,\npouring out your fury and making them drunk\nso you can look at their nakedness!|Preserves the source’s person shifts and sexual exposure; notes fury/poison ambiguity.

2:16|You are filled with disgrace instead of glory.
Drink, you too, and expose your uncircumcision!
The cup in the LORD’s right hand will come around to you,
and filthy shame will cover your glory.|Retains the pinned uncircumcision image and the shame/glory reversal.

2:17|For the violence done to Lebanon will engulf you,
as will the destruction of animals that terrified them,
because of human bloodshed and violence against the land,
the city, and all who live in it.|Restores a readable parallel clause while retaining the difficult animals/them pronoun and the explicit cause.

2:18|What use is a carved image that its maker carved,
a cast image that teaches lies?
Its maker trusts his own creation,
making idols that cannot speak.|Keeps the maker/made recurrence and mute idols in natural syntax.

2:19|Woe to the one who tells wood, ‘Wake up!’
and a silent stone, ‘Get up!’
Can it teach?
Look, it is coated with gold and silver,
but there is no breath at all inside it.|Retains direct absurd commands and the contrast of costly covering and absent breath.
2:20|But the LORD is in his holy temple.\nLet all the earth be silent before him.”|Keeps the contrast with mute idols and universal silence.
3:1|A prayer of Habakkuk the prophet, according to Shigionoth.|Preserves the uncertain performance term rather than inventing a musical description.

3:3|God comes from Teman,
the Holy One from Mount Paran. Selah.
His splendor covers the heavens;
his praise fills the earth.|Preserves locations, the divine appearance, and the performance marker.
3:4|His brightness is like light;\nrays flash from his hand,\nand there his power is hidden.|Renders horns as rays in the light context and notes the literal image.
3:5|Plague goes before him,\nand pestilence follows at his feet.|Retains the personified attendants without adding mythological identities.
3:7|I see the tents of Cushan under affliction;\nthe tent curtains of Midian tremble.|Retains Cushan as written and the parallel tent images.

3:8|Was the LORD angry with the rivers?
Was your anger against the rivers,
your fury against the sea,
when you rode your horses,
your chariots of salvation?|Keeps the shift into direct address and the repeated question rather than explaining it away.

3:9|You draw your bow bare—\noaths, rods, a word. Selah.\nYou split the earth with rivers.|Preserves the very uncertain middle words in a restrained rendering with an explicit note, not a confident invented scene.

3:10|The mountains see you and writhe;
a torrent of water sweeps past.
The deep raises its voice
and lifts its hands high.|Keeps the natural world’s bodily personification.
3:11|Sun and moon stand still in their dwelling\nat the light of your flying arrows,\nat the gleam of your flashing spear.|Retains celestial stillness and both divine weapons.
3:12|In indignation you march through the earth;\nin anger you thresh the nations.|Keeps the agricultural violence image and parallel emotions.

3:13|You go out to save your people,
to save your anointed one.
You crush the head of the wicked house,
laying it bare from foundation to neck. Selah.|Retains the unnamed anointed one and mixed house/body image without harmonizing it.

3:14|With his own shafts you pierce the head of his warriors,\nwho storm out to scatter me,\ndelighting as though to devour the poor in hiding.|Follows the read plural warriors and preserves me and the predatory comparison.
3:15|You tread through the sea with your horses,\nthrough the surge of mighty waters.|Retains the mounted divine action and turbulent waters.

3:16|I hear, and my body trembles;
at the sound my lips quiver.
Decay enters my bones,
and my legs shake beneath me.
Yet I will wait quietly for the day of distress
to come upon the people who raid us.|Unfolds bodily fear into readable clauses and records the difficult final expectation without overclaiming certainty.

3:17|Though the fig tree does not blossom
and there is no fruit on the vines,
though the olive crop fails
and the fields produce no food,
though the flock is cut off from the pen
and there are no cattle in the stalls,|Keeps all six losses and lets the concessive sentence continue into the next verse.
3:18|yet I will celebrate in the LORD;\nI will rejoice in the God who saves me.|Retains the first-person resolve and double rejoicing despite the preceding losses.

3:19|The LORD, the Lord, is my strength.
He makes my feet like a deer’s
and leads me on my heights.
For the music leader, with my stringed instruments.|Preserves both divine designations, personal heights, and the final performance direction inside its verse.
